cards.back: A process of planned educational interventions with socially maladjusted people, aimed at changing attitudes and behaviour so that they can fulfil social roles independently and constructively.

cards.front: Social maladjustment – whose concepts and what is it?
cards.back: A concept developed in Polish resocialization pedagogy by, among others, Czesław Czapów and Lesław Pytka. It denotes a relatively persistent pattern of norm-violating behaviour that hampers the fulfilment of social roles.
A concept by Marek Konopczyński. It uses creative activities (e.g. theatre, music, sport, art) to develop the person's potential and build a new, prosocial identity.
The deficit approach focuses on shortcomings and disorders, whereas the resource-based approach builds interventions on strengths, interests and support available in the person's environment.
Re-adjustment of a person to independent life in society after a period of isolation, e.g. after leaving prison or an institution – covering housing, work and relationships, among others.
Support for people leaving prison and their families (e.g. housing, material, vocational, legal), intended to ease readaptation and reduce reoffending.
Edwin Lemert and Howard Becker. Social reaction and attaching a 'deviant' label can entrench deviant behaviour and reshape the person's identity.
Lemert's distinction: primary deviance is incidental norm-breaking that does not affect identity; secondary deviance arises when the person adopts the label and organises behaviour around it.
Edwin Sutherland. Criminal behaviour – its techniques, motives and rationalisations – is learned through interaction within close personal groups.

cards.front: Anomie (strain) theory – author and modes of adaptation
cards.back: Robert K. Merton. Tension between cultural goals and available institutional means leads to modes of adaptation: conformity, innovation, ritualism, retreatism and rebellion.

cards.front: Social bond theory – author and elements
cards.back: Travis Hirschi. Bonds to society protect against offending: attachment, commitment (to conventional goals), involvement (in conventional activities) and belief (acceptance of norms).
Albert Bandura. Behaviours, including aggression, are acquired through observing and imitating models, among other ways, and maintained by reinforcement.
Don Andrews and James Bonta. Principles: risk (intensity matched to risk level), need (targeting criminogenic needs) and responsivity (methods matched to the person's abilities and learning style).
Dynamic – i.e. changeable – risk factors linked to offending, e.g. pro-criminal attitudes, associating with people who offend, substance use, unemployment.

Static factors cannot change (e.g. age at first offence, criminal history); dynamic factors can be changed through intervention (e.g. attitudes, skills, environment), so they are the target of resocialization work.

cards.front: Good Lives Model – author and essence
cards.back: Tony Ward. It assumes people pursue primary goods (e.g. relationships, competence, autonomy) and that work should help them achieve these prosocially, not merely reduce risk.
The gradual process of ceasing offending and sustaining a crime-free life. Shadd Maruna described the role of identity narratives (the 'redemption script') in this process.

cards.front: Aggression Replacement Training (ART) – author and components
cards.back: A programme developed by Arnold P. Goldstein and colleagues. Three components: prosocial skills training, anger control training and moral reasoning training.

An approach (developed by Howard Zehr, among others) in which the response to crime focuses on repairing harm and relationships with the involvement of victim, offender and community, e.g. through mediation.

cards.front: Systems of serving a prison sentence (Poland)
cards.back: The Polish Executive Penal Code provides three systems: programmed influence, therapeutic and ordinary.
A system in which a person serving a sentence, with their consent, follows an individual programme prepared with their participation (e.g. education, work, therapy, family contact).

Identifying problems and deficits as well as the strengths of the person and their environment, explaining the mechanisms of maladjustment, and formulating a prognosis and basis for an individual plan.
Enforces court decisions and carries out supervision, combining monitoring with educational, resocialization and support activities; Poland has family and adult probation officers.
An education-system facility for socially maladjusted children and adolescents, placed there by a family court decision; it combines schooling with educational interventions.
An education facility for children and adolescents at risk of social maladjustment who need sociotherapy and special organisation of learning.
A correctional facility (zakład poprawczy) carries out a court-ordered correctional measure; a juvenile shelter (schronisko) is for temporary placement while proceedings are ongoing.
An informal system of norms, hierarchies and rituals among people in custody that can hinder resocialization efforts and foster violence.
Activities addressed to whole populations (e.g. all pupils in a class) regardless of individual risk; the aim is to prevent or delay initiation.
Activities for groups at elevated risk because of their life situation or environment (e.g. children from families with alcohol problems), before problems appear.
Activities for individuals already showing early signs or risk behaviours (e.g. experimenting with substances) but without a diagnosis of dependence.
Robert Gordon (1983); it was popularised by, among others, the 1994 Institute of Medicine report.
Older classification: primary prevents the problem from occurring, secondary detects and limits it early, tertiary prevents worsening and relapse and supports reintegration.
Characteristics of a person or their environment that increase the likelihood of problem behaviour, e.g. family conflict, school failure, peers who use substances, easy access to substances.

Characteristics of a person or environment that reduce the likelihood of problem behaviour or buffer risk factors, e.g. strong bond with parents, interest in school, prosocial norms and groups, social skills.
The capacity for positive adaptation and healthy development despite adverse circumstances; strengthening its factors is one of the goals of prevention.

Richard Jessor. Risk behaviours (e.g. substance use, early sexual initiation, truancy) tend to co-occur and serve developmental functions for young people, so it is worth addressing their shared determinants.
Commonly listed: information, education (skill-building), alternatives, intervention, harm reduction, and environmental and policy change.
Providing knowledge about harm alone usually does not change behaviour, and fear-based messages can be ineffective or counterproductive; information works better as part of a broader programme.
Correcting young people's beliefs that substance use among peers is more common and accepted than it really is.
Programmes that teach recognising and coping with peer, media and advertising pressure (e.g. assertive refusal), often combined with normative education.
Abilities for positive behaviour and coping with challenges, e.g. decision-making, problem-solving, critical thinking, communication, coping with stress and emotions.
A school-based universal substance-use prevention programme for pupils aged about 12–14, based on the social influence model and life skills; delivered as interactive lessons.

A joint system of central institutions (incl. KCPU and ORE) that assesses programmes for quality and evidence of effectiveness; recommended programmes are listed in a database for schools and local governments.
Standards developed under the auspices of the EMCDDA describing the prevention project cycle: from needs assessment, through planning and delivery, to evaluation.
Based on needs assessment and theory, interactive methods, adequate intensity and continuity, age- and culture-appropriateness, involvement of parents and community, and evaluation.
Process evaluation checks how a programme was delivered (reach, fidelity, reception); outcome evaluation assesses whether intended changes in participants were achieved.
An approach that reduces the health and social consequences of substance use without requiring abstinence as a condition of help, e.g. needle and syringe programmes or opioid agonist treatment.
Changing the conditions in which people make decisions, e.g. limiting the physical and economic availability of alcohol, enforcing bans on sales to minors, shaping local norms.
Elements of a brief intervention: Feedback, Responsibility, Advice, Menu of options, Empathy, Self-efficacy.
Prompt recognition of the first signs of a problem (e.g. first episodes of use) and taking adequate action before the problem becomes entrenched.
Trained young leaders, supported by adults, run activities among their peers, drawing on their credibility and normative influence.
The WHO Ottawa Charter (1986): health promotion is the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health.
Offering attractive, prosocial ways of meeting needs (e.g. adventure, recognition, belonging) – sport, volunteering, creative activities – best combined with other strategies.

cards.front: Needs assessment before a prevention programme
cards.back: Identifying problems, risk and protective factors and resources in a group or community; it guides the choice of prevention level, goals and methods and provides a baseline for evaluation.

cards.front: Substance dependence in ICD-11 – three core features
cards.back: Impaired control over use; increasing precedence of use over other activities and obligations despite harm; physiological features (tolerance, withdrawal). Usually at least two are required for the diagnosis.
A pattern of substance use that causes damage to physical or mental health (and in ICD-11 also harm to others), without meeting the criteria for dependence.
A state in which increasing amounts of a substance are needed to achieve the same effect, or the same amount produces a weaker effect.
A cluster of physical and psychological symptoms that appear after stopping or reducing a substance used long-term; some (e.g. with alcohol) can be life-threatening and need medical care.
A strong desire or urge to use a substance, often triggered by cues associated with use; its appearance is not a failure but a signal to apply coping strategies.

cards.front: Psychological mechanisms of addiction – author and names
cards.back: Jerzy Mellibruda: the mechanism of addictive emotion regulation, the mechanism of illusions and denial, and the mechanism of a scattered and split self.

A view in which biological (e.g. genetic, neurobiological), psychological (e.g. emotion regulation) and social (e.g. family, environment, availability) factors jointly shape the development and maintenance of addiction.
Substances and some behaviours strongly activate the brain's reward system (incl. the mesolimbic pathway, dopamine), which promotes learning of cue–use associations and weakens control.
James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente. It describes behaviour change as moving through stages: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance (with possible relapse).
The person does not intend to change in the foreseeable future (typically the next 6 months) and often sees no problem; building rapport, accurate information and non-confrontational dialogue help.
The person recognises the problem and considers change but is ambivalent – seeing both benefits and costs of change; exploring ambivalence and building motivation help.
The person intends to take action soon (typically within a month) and often takes first steps; jointly developing a concrete change plan helps.
In action the person actively changes behaviour; in maintenance (after about 6 months) they consolidate change and prevent relapse. Support focuses on coping skills and reinforcing gains.
Relapse is seen as a common part of the change process rather than failure; the person may return to an earlier stage and use the experience in the next attempt.
G. Alan Marlatt and Judith Gordon. A cognitive-behavioural model: relapse results from the interplay of high-risk situations, coping skills, self-efficacy and outcome expectancies.
A lapse is a single episode of use after a period of abstinence or reduction; relapse is a return to the previous problematic pattern. Responding well to a lapse can prevent relapse.
Marlatt's term for a reaction to a lapse: guilt and attributing it to stable, internal causes ('I'm weak, I can't do it'), which increases the risk of a lapse turning into relapse.
Negative emotional states, interpersonal conflict and social pressure; others include positive emotions, testing personal control and craving.
Small choices that seem unrelated to use (e.g. a route home past a former drinking place) but gradually bring the person closer to a high-risk situation.
Albert Bandura's concept: a person's belief that they can cope with a specific difficult situation; higher self-efficacy is associated with lower relapse risk.
Terence Gorski (CENAPS model) described relapse as a process in which changes in thinking, emotions and behaviour precede a return to use; people learn to recognise and interrupt them.

Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention (Sarah Bowen, Neha Chawla, G. Alan Marlatt) combines relapse prevention with mindfulness practice, teaching people to observe craving and emotions without reacting automatically.
In the group of disorders due to addictive behaviours, ICD-11 lists gambling disorder and gaming disorder.

cards.front: Other behaviours described as behavioural addictions
cards.back: E.g. problematic internet and social media use, compulsive buying or work; they have no separate ICD-11 category, and compulsive sexual behaviour disorder is classified there as an impulse control disorder.
A model of addiction treatment combining professional (mainly group) therapy with the 12-step programme; the goal is abstinence and people are encouraged to join mutual-help groups.
Alcoholics Anonymous was founded in 1935 in the USA; it is based on the 12 steps and mutual support. Similar fellowships exist for other addictions (e.g. NA, GA) and for families (Al-Anon).
Co-occurrence of substance use disorders and other mental disorders (e.g. depression, anxiety); it requires integrated, coordinated care.
For some people (especially without severe dependence) the goal may be reducing and controlling drinking rather than full abstinence; the goal is set individually together with a specialist.

cards.front: Act on Upbringing in Sobriety and Counteracting Alcoholism – date
cards.back: Act of 26 October 1982; it governs, among other things, prevention and resolving alcohol problems, rules on alcohol sales and advertising, and compulsory treatment.

cards.front: Act on Counteracting Drug Addiction – date
cards.back: Act of 29 July 2005; it governs prevention, treatment, rehabilitation and harm reduction, as well as substance control and criminal liability.

cards.front: Act on Supporting and Resocializing Juveniles – when did it enter into force?
cards.back: 1 September 2022. It replaced the 1982 Act on Juvenile Proceedings.

cards.front: Act on Supporting and Resocializing Juveniles – who it covers
cards.back: It covers, among others, preventing and addressing demoralisation of persons under 18 and proceedings for punishable acts committed by persons aged 10 to under 17.

E.g. a reprimand, an obligation to behave in a specific way, responsible parental supervision, probation officer supervision, placement in a youth educational centre (MOW), and as a correctional measure – placement in a correctional facility.
Act of 29 July 2005, renamed by a 2023 amendment (previously: on counteracting family violence), which broadened the definition of violence, e.g. to include economic violence and cyberviolence.
A procedure for intervening where domestic violence is reasonably suspected; it is initiated by a representative of an authorised service by completing the 'Blue Card – A' form.

cards.front: Who can initiate the Blue Card procedure?
cards.back: Representatives of: social assistance units, municipal commissions for solving alcohol problems, the Police, education and healthcare.
The municipality appoints an interdisciplinary team to counter domestic violence; individual cases are handled by diagnostic-support groups (since 2023, replacing working groups).

cards.front: Measures protecting a person experiencing domestic violence – examples
cards.back: E.g. an order to leave the shared home immediately and a restraining order, which may be issued by the Police (or Military Police) and then reviewed by a court.

cards.front: KCPU – what is it and since when?
cards.back: The National Centre for Counteracting Addictions, operating since 1 January 2022; it took over the tasks of PARPA and the National Bureau for Drug Prevention and is responsible for policy on substance and behavioural addictions.
The State Agency for Solving Alcohol Problems and the National Bureau for Drug Prevention – central institutions dissolved at the end of 2021, whose tasks were taken over by KCPU.

The municipal commission for solving alcohol problems initiates prevention activities, gives opinions on alcohol sales licences as to compliance with municipal council resolutions, and takes steps towards court-ordered treatment.

cards.front: Municipal programme for prevention and solving alcohol problems – funding
cards.back: The municipality runs it as its own task; it is funded from fees for alcohol sales licences.
For persons who, in connection with alcohol misuse, cause the breakdown of family life or demoralisation of minors, evade work, or systematically disturb public peace or order.

cards.front: Compulsory treatment – who decides and on whose request?
cards.back: The district court competent for the person's place of residence, usually at the request of the municipal commission for solving alcohol problems or a prosecutor, with expert opinions.
Selling or serving alcoholic beverages is prohibited to persons under 18, to persons whose behaviour indicates intoxication, and on credit or as a pledge.
Advertising and promotion of alcoholic beverages is generally prohibited, except for beer, which may be advertised subject to statutory restrictions.
The Act on Counteracting Drug Addiction criminalises possession of narcotic and psychotropic substances; in certain cases (e.g. a small amount for personal use) proceedings may be discontinued.

cards.front: 'Treatment instead of punishment' in the drug act
cards.back: The act provides mechanisms allowing a dependent person facing criminal proceedings to undertake treatment, which may affect the proceedings, e.g. lead to their suspension.
Act of 27 July 2001; it sets out the organisation of the court probation service and the rights and duties of family and adult probation officers.

cards.front: Executive Penal Code – what does it regulate?
cards.back: Enforcement of criminal judgments, including imprisonment (and the systems for serving it), restriction of liberty, probation supervision and post-penitentiary assistance.
A way of serving a prison sentence (in specified cases) outside prison, at the convicted person's place of residence, with electronic monitoring of their whereabouts.
Act of 12 March 2004; it defines the tasks and forms of social assistance and the institutions, including municipal social assistance centres and county family support centres (PCPR).
Act of 19 August 1994; it governs, among other things, the provision of psychiatric care, including admission to hospital without consent in situations specified by the act.
Following a 2023 amendment, schools, facilities and other organisations working with children must adopt standards protecting minors from harm (from 2024).
Juvenile cases are heard by the family court (the family and juvenile division of the district court).
William R. Miller and Stephen Rollnick.
A collaborative, goal-oriented style of conversation with particular attention to the language of change, strengthening personal motivation and commitment by eliciting the person's own reasons.
Partnership, acceptance, compassion (commitment to the person's welfare) and evocation; in the fourth edition (2023) evocation was replaced by empowerment.

cards.front: Partnership in the spirit of MI
cards.back: Working 'with' rather than 'on' the person: both are experts – the practitioner in knowledge, the person in their own life.

cards.front: Acceptance in the spirit of MI – four aspects
cards.back: Absolute worth, accurate empathy, autonomy support and affirmation (recognising strengths and efforts).
Assumes that motivation and resources for change already exist within the person; the practitioner's task is to draw them out rather than insert their own arguments.
Engaging (building the relationship), focusing (agreeing on direction), evoking (drawing out motivation for change) and planning (developing commitment and a plan).

cards.front: OARS – what does it stand for?
cards.back: Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections and Summaries – the core MI skills.
Questions inviting broader answers and reflection (e.g. 'What makes you think about changing?'), as opposed to closed questions answered with 'yes/no' or briefly.
Genuine recognition of the person's specific strengths, values or efforts (e.g. 'Despite a hard week you came – that shows it matters to you'), rather than general praise.
A simple reflection repeats or slightly rephrases what was said; a complex reflection adds meaning, e.g. names a feeling or implied sense, and usually moves the conversation forward more.
Reflects both sides of ambivalence, e.g. 'On the one hand drinking helps you relax, and on the other you worry about your health'; best ending with the change side.
Reflecting a sustain-talk statement in a slightly exaggerated form, without sarcasm, which often prompts the person to balance their position and voice change talk.
Collecting (gather several statements), linking (connect a current statement with an earlier one) and transitional (close one part of the conversation and move to the next).
Preparatory: Desire, Ability, Reasons, Need; mobilising: Commitment, Activation, Taking steps.
Preparatory talk expresses motivation ('I'd like to', 'I could', 'I should'); mobilising talk signals moving into action ('I will', 'I'm ready', 'this week I already…').
Statements favouring keeping the behaviour unchanged (e.g. 'Drinking doesn't harm me'); a natural part of ambivalence, not resistance to be overcome.

Tension in the relationship between practitioner and person (e.g. arguing, interrupting, disengaging); in newer MI editions it replaced part of the meaning of 'resistance' and signals the practitioner to change approach.
The helper's natural urge to persuade, advise and 'fix' the problem; it usually prompts an ambivalent person to defend the status quo, so MI practitioners resist it.
Asking for a 0–10 rating of how important change is and how confident the person is, then: 'Why this number and not lower?' and 'What would help raise it by one point?'.
A way of sharing information in MI: ask what the person knows or wants to know, provide information (with permission, neutrally), ask what they make of it.
Simultaneously feeling motivation for and against change; seen as a normal step on the way to change, to be explored rather than fought.
Helping the person see the gap between current behaviour and their important values and goals, which can strengthen motivation to change.

cards.front: The four MI principles from earlier editions
cards.back: Expressing empathy, developing discrepancy, rolling with resistance (avoiding argumentation) and supporting self-efficacy.
The question-answer trap, expert trap, labelling trap, premature focus trap, blaming trap and chat trap – they hinder engagement.

cards.front: Techniques for evoking change talk – examples
cards.back: Evocative questions, rulers, querying extremes ('What's the worst that could happen?'), looking back and looking forward, and exploring values and goals.
Motivational Interviewing Treatment Integrity – a tool for coding recorded sessions to assess MI fidelity and develop practitioner skills.

A persistent pattern of thoughts, emotions and behaviours in a family member that develops through long-term life with an addicted person (e.g. excessive control, taking over responsibility, self-neglect); understood as adaptation to chronic stress, not an illness.

cards.front: Typical behaviours of relatives of a person with an alcohol problem
cards.back: Controlling drinking, hiding the problem from others, making excuses, taking over duties, cushioning the consequences of drinking – which may unintentionally maintain the problem.

cards.front: Children's roles in a family with alcohol problems – author
cards.back: Sharon Wegscheider-Cruse: the family hero, scapegoat, lost child and mascot; alongside them the 'enabler' role (often the drinking person's partner) is described.
Often the eldest child: responsible, high-achieving, a source of family pride, but often at the cost of their own needs and emotions.
A child who, through difficult behaviour (rebellion, school problems), draws the family's attention and tension, diverting it from the drinking problem.
A withdrawn, quiet, 'invisible' child who avoids conflict and causes no trouble but may be isolated and overlooked.
A child who relieves tension through humour and clowning; draws attention and lightens the mood but may struggle to express real feelings.

cards.front: 'Don't talk, don't trust, don't feel' – author
cards.back: Claudia Black described these unwritten rules of families with alcohol problems, which teach children silence about the problem, mistrust and suppressing feelings.
Adults who grew up in families with alcohol problems, whose childhood experiences may affect adult functioning; it is not a diagnosis. Described by, among others, Janet Woititz.

cards.front: CRAFT – what it stands for and authors
cards.back: Community Reinforcement and Family Training – an approach developed by Robert J. Meyers and colleagues (incl. Jane Ellen Smith, Brenda L. Wolfe) for relatives of people who refuse treatment.
Improving the well-being and functioning of family members, reducing the person's substance use and increasing the chance that they will enter treatment.
Functional analysis of use, positive communication, rewarding substance-free behaviour, allowing natural consequences of use, self-care, safety planning and choosing the moment to invite treatment.
In comparative studies CRAFT led to treatment entry more often than confrontational intervention or referral to Al-Anon, while placing less strain on the relationship.
Where there is violence in the family, the safety of those experiencing it (safety plan, Blue Card procedure) comes before work on the drinking person's motivation.

A model by Jim Orford and colleagues: living with a relative who uses substances causes stress and strain; family members cope by engaging, tolerating or withdrawing; social support buffers the effects.
A brief intervention for family members (Copello, Orford, Velleman et al.): listening, providing information, exploring coping, developing social support and arranging further help.
A graphic record of family structure, usually covering at least three generations, with key events and relationships; the notation was popularised by Monica McGoldrick and Randy Gerson.

A square stands for a male, a circle for a female, an X in the symbol for death; horizontal lines connect partners, vertical lines lead to children, and special lines show relationship quality (e.g. closeness, conflict).
Ann Hartman (1978). It shows the family in the context of its environment – institutions, people and groups – revealing sources of support and stress and the flow of resources.
A solid line means a strong, supportive tie, a dashed line a weak one, and a hatched line a stressful or conflictual relationship; arrows show the direction of energy or resource flow.
The family is seen as a system of interconnected people; one member's problem affects everyone and may serve a function in maintaining the system's balance.
Don D. Jackson. The family's tendency to maintain its existing balance, even if dysfunctional, which can make change difficult.
Salvador Minuchin (structural therapy): boundaries can be clear, rigid (fostering disengagement) or diffuse (fostering enmeshment).
Role reversal in which a child takes on duties and emotional responsibility appropriate for adults; the concept was introduced by Iván Böszörményi-Nagy.
David H. Olson. It describes family functioning along the dimensions of cohesion and flexibility, with communication as a facilitating dimension.
Al-Anon – a fellowship for relatives of people with alcohol problems; Alateen – for teenagers. They offer support regardless of whether the drinking person enters treatment.

cards.front: Protective factors for children in families with alcohol problems
cards.back: E.g. at least one stable, supportive adult, predictable family rituals, age-appropriate accurate information about the problem and support outside the home (school, day-care centre, group).
